newsitem.title: USA: US corporate bonds firm, Penn Traffic jams in junk.
newsitem.headline: US corporate bonds firm, Penn Traffic jams in junk.

text.p: U.S. investment-grade corporate bonds garnered firm bids and spreads were unchanged to marginally tighter on Friday in thin activity ahead of what could be a turbulent week, traders said.

Dull high-yield trade was punctuated by brisk downtrades for Penn Traffic debt following news the supermarket's same-store sales dropped an "unheard of" 8.5 percent in December, junk traders and analysts said.
Penn Traffic's 9.625 percent bonds due 2005 fell eight points since Tuesday to a 49 bid late on Friday, traders said.
The company's stock fell 5/8 to 2-3/4 on Friday.

Away from Penn Traffic, high-yielders were characterized as firm and thinly traded. Most bonds outperformed stagnant U.S. Treasuries for the second consecutive session, dealers said, with prices edging higher by 1/4 point on average.
Both investment grades and high-yield dealers were poised for a busy session on Monday when fixed-income markets are expected to go full-tilt after two weeks of holiday trading.
"It will be interesting to see if people take profits or if people have nowhere else to go with their cash," said a trader at a big New York shop.

Investment grade activity was again thin and mostly limited to institutional accounts, traders said. Moderate actvity surrounded some trust preferred deals, however, with yield spreads narrowly mixed on the day.

Citicorp, Chase, and JPM Capital Trust's preferred issues garnered the best interest among recent deals. The near-term outlook for the securities was uncertain, however, with the investor masses returning in full force on Monday.
"I think the consensus here is to lighten up a touch in here and prepare for new supply coming," said one bank and finance trader, adding that the calendar should amass soon.
In addition, profit-taking may be the preferred course of action next week given the 20 to 25 basis point tightening enjoyed by the bulk of the securities late last year.

The recent back-up in government yields was an ominous cloud over the corporate market, dealers said. Treasury prices fell on the week following separate reports of strong manufacturing, construction and consumer confidence.
"There is buying (in corporates) but it's not full-guns yet, at least in retail" one trader said. "This year may be starting out tough."

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond closed up 2/32 at 97 to yield 6.73 percent. The T-bond's yield fell to 6.70 percent at midday based, according to some analysts, on talk that Japanese accounts would be heavy buyers of U.S. government securities when trading resumes on Monday.
